Solving Schrodingers paradox using computational complexity theory.

This was interesting until you get to:

There are well known quantum states that do contain Avogadro’s number of particles: these include superfluids, supeconductors, lasers and so on.

Which sort of disproves the theory, at least from what I've read. Unfortunately I'm not a physicist, maybe one could have told you this up front.
You have a point, but even though the theory is incomplete, the reasoning is really interesting.

With those systems we have some additional information about what's going on. I'm most familiar with lasers, in which we can take shortcuts based on allowed states of the photons. All of these examples seem akin to saying solve this traveling salesman problem: find the most efficient path from Mediterranean ave to boardwalk with no minimum step size.

The physical systems aren't quite so simple as a monopoly board, but special cases can allow for much easier computation.
I do not get the example - maybe I lack the reference to mediterranean ave and boardwalk. Also got confused by the lack of min step size. May you explain more?

In the game Monopoly (http://www.proprofs.com/quiz-school/user_upload/ckeditor/monopoly_original.jpg) the first property off the line is Mediterranean ave. and the last is Boardwalk. The problem is that if you roll a pair of dice, the smallest step size is 2 tiles. By saying no minimum step size, I'm saying you may take the properties one at a time. It would be trivial to figure out the most efficient route of going to every property in the game in this case: is the next tile one the salesman should go to? If so, go to it, if not, skip it.

The physics is rarely reduced to that simple of a problem, but superfluidity, superconduction, and laser systems all have shortcuts which should allow them to be P problems, rather than NP problems.

What was a time that Linux exceeded your expectations?

I was really impressed when I revived my father's ~10 year old laptop using Xubuntu. Because, contrary to Windows, the Linux ecosystems tends not to pile on more crap every year, hardware that is 5-6 years old is still perfectly fine for daily use now, if you don't game or anything.

I myself can do all my daily business using a '08 Thinkpad with a Core 2 Duo and 2G memory. Works fine, browsing with Firefox, having dozens of open tabs, YouTube videos in HD, no sweat. And for my heavy duty compiling I just have a headless 16-core machine sitting in my basement that I wake up over LAN whenever I need some raw power, and send it back to sleep afterwards.

EDIT: Also when a close friend of mine managed to build a Windows VM with working PCIe passthrough for his graphics card. While it was in my opinion pointless, it was very impressive from a technical point of view that he could get close to bare metal performance. He used it for CAD and gaming without having to dual-boot.

My girlfriend's family would always bring me random computers and phones so I could fix them for free (/sigh).

One time, they brought me their nephew's old laptop that he would use for watching DVDs. I was aware of this kid's home life, and knew his parents were kinda shit, didn't have much money, and didn't really pay attention to him. I don't remember the exact problem, but the laptop didn't work anymore. They said they even took it to the Geek Squad (lol) and they couldn't fix it. Within a couple hours, I had a fresh linux install on there. It ran exponentially faster, got DVDs working again, and I also downloaded him a bunch of ROMs and emulators and gave him an old Xbox 360 controller just for funsies. You should have seen that little kids face when I gave it back to him.

Haha. Nah, that's more MY newphew's reaction to things. Like when I set up a Minecraft server for him (after he wouldn't stop asking about it for weeks) and his response is "cool. what's the ip?"

Kids these days..
Just did the same thing with a very old laptop at work. 2002 Compaq - using it to read some old floppy discs we have.

That's what got me into Linux in the first place. My old laptop was running slow thanks to windows bloat, and I didn't want to buy a new one just to have the same thing happen. Swapped to Xubuntu and never looked back.

15+ years ago when I installed Mandrake and realised I didn't need to pirate Windows 98 to surf the net ;)

To be honest, it exceeds everyday when it saves me hours every week in admin duties due to the opensource nature of Linux (or Debian if we're being specific)
When all of my (not really all that old) hardware that Windows 7 wouldn't allow to run, ran just fine under Linux. TV card, USB devices like USB hubs, Video capture adapter etc..
Most recently: booting up fat dog 64 (a version of puppy Linux) and seeing it find my multi-touch touchscreen. Also, the multi – layered file system technology is just crazy.

Before I tried Linux, I had gotten really good at disabling services and other bits of Windows to eek out every last drop of power and disk space. Don't own a printer so I uninstall printer drivers and disable the spooler and related shit. Anything that I would like to keep if my hard drive took a bullet already gets saved to either my externals, one of multiple cloud services, or all of the above, so shadow copy and the whole restore thing gets shut off.

I had whittled windows down from a 20 gig beast that ate ram like it was going out of style to a 12 gig beat that sipped a mere 800 mb or so with no third party stuff running. I knew I wasn't the best but I figured that was pretty damn good.

Then I tried Ubuntu. 7 something (don't remember if it was LTS or not), and seeing it run FROM RAM and only use about 200 mb I was astonished. I didn't think it was possible outside of the specialized OS one would see on a gaming console. I fell in love that day.
To this day, I still don't know how Windows can eat that much ram.
By having every driver for every possible piece of hardware installed and running all the time. It's brutally dumb.
I was able to install Arch on an old laptop my dad owned (Thinkpad T41, for the curious) with zero issues. It runs XFCE just fine, as well as most of the programs I throw at it.
Hardware support has always been fantastic in my experience.

I got Ubuntu 8 from an ex-brother-in-law. He could not figure out how to play videos. This was when ubuntu was damn near bare for a lifelong windows user with no pc background,and only wanting to watch videos. (I still am now, just good enough to solve most issues, or know where to ask ?) I found a few youtube vids on my laptop and was able to get youtube up and a few drivers to get everything going. It seemed easy, yet a bit challenging. The terminal intimidated me at first, but after playing around and breaking it beyond restore cd's, I was hooked.
Package managers. Being able to ask the system to install any particular software and have it automatically install dependencies for you is unheard of in Windows.

I've got a bunch of these:

  • the first time I used a live CD, and realised I could start a fully working OS on pretty much any system from a CD without needing to worry about drivers
  • when I realised I could use Pulseaudio to stream audio between a Linux and Windows system, and the longest part of the process was downloading the Windows client
  • when I tried gaming through WINE, and found that more often than not, the games I wanted to play were listed in appdb with all the relevant workarounds
  • btrfs snapshots - incremental backups that take less than a second to create - completely blew me away
  • multiseat setup - despite being poorly documented, I was able to get it working (using systemd-logind and pulseaudio) in only a few days, and it basically just works.
  • /proc/config.gz - was not expecting that to exist. Really convenient, when you need it.
  • moving drives between systems and seeing it just boot. Windows required a re-install, but Linux worked fine pretty much everywhere, except in one case where a specialised kernel was needed (due to some issue with ACPI), and I could still select the old kernel through GRUB.

Data recovery. I've had drives recently that seemed to have just dropped their partition tables, and all the recommended (even paid) programs on Windows might see the old tables but couldn't do a thing to recover them. I plug the drive into my computer (Fedora) and it immediately sees the drive, windows partitions, and can access all the data without a hiccup. Recovered my wife's desktop that way.

Installing Linux on an originally XP laptop that for some reason can no longer handle it, but works fine with a lightweight distro.

Also, being able to send raw GPS data over bluetooth from my phone to a bluetooth dongle on the laptop and piping it for use with other programs. Very fun.

The most recent time, was using it to replace Windows 7 on my neighbor's laptop. He used to get his Windows infected with all sorts of nasties (mostly by installing "free" programs that promised all sorts of things - he's pretty dumb) once or twice a month. After over a year of redoing his laptop and trying to protect him from his own stupidity, I got him to try Linux. No more viruses, spyware, or anything else.

He installed some crapware via Wine (without realizing it) the other month and called me because "this browser I installed doesn't work". I deleted the files from his Wine folder and informed him that Linux protected him from what used to happen to his Windows system. I think he finally realises that he doesn't "need" anything to keep his system working.

So, out of the many times Linux has exceeded my expectations, this is the biggest one. When people find out that you know a good deal about computers, everyone wants you to be their tech support. Linux makes it so that you don't have to do much support.
Back in the day when I couldn't use Wifi on my laptop, because nobody seemed to know where to get Windows XP drivers for my old laptop's Wifi card adapter, but on Ubuntu it worked automatically.
Using a live cd for the first time. That blew me away.

I work as a designer in the sign industry, and I can definitely see it having a huge impact once the technology has reached certain milestones.

The first issue for our industry that needs to be addressed is durability. We make sign faces from polycarbonate because the stuff is relatively cheap and so damn hard to break. But it's also a pain to work with at certain sizes. To do large sign faces, the material has to be cured for 2 days, then heated and placed on a huge vacuum press and formed into a pan shape for rigidity. Then it has to have graphics applied or be painted.

The graphics are printed on a large, expensive machine and have to be laminated which requires another large, expensive machine. Or, if you're painting them, a paint booth is required and there are fire hazard and environmental regulations that are involved.

The whole process is labor intensive, expensive, and has some pretty negative environmental impacts. Being able to print large, durable, and impact resistant sign faces will reduce the physical footprint of a sign shop, reduce the energy and labor involved and be much better for the environment, but the technology isn't quite there yet. That will likely change within my lifetime.
How do you think 3D Printing will affect industry in the future?

I think it can do a lot of wonders and I hope it gets the chance to. The problem is that it's also going to cut down production costs and the like. So it's going to cost a lot of people a lot of money and even cost people jobs. I hope we can get past all of that but I'm not so sure.
